claims.text: W particles or connected W regions should be precoated with a thin Ni film before Cu infiltration or sintering.
A Ni interlayer will improve wetting and bonding at the W–Cu interface relative to processing without an interlayer.
Improved wetting and bonding from the Ni interlayer will reduce interfacial void formation.
The Ni interlayer will reduce phase separation in the W–Cu composite.
The Ni-modified interface will preserve mechanical durability under irradiation.
Conventionally fabricated W–Cu composites have significant interfacial voids and poor wetting that impair thermal transport and mechanical integrity.
Vapor deposition or sputtering can provide a thin, uniform Ni film on W particles or regions before infiltration.
The Ni interlayer remains suitable when processing is kept below approximately 1100–1300 °C.
Fusion divertor components operate under high thermal flux.
Interlayers are relevant to joining W plasma-facing material with Cu-based cooling components because of their different working-temperature requirements.
A Ni interlayer reduces interfacial-energy differences at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni layer lowers the energy barrier for Cu wetting and infiltration into a W framework.
Enhanced Cu infiltration caused by the Ni layer promotes complete filling of microvoids.
The Ni-mediated interface reduces phase separation during cooling.
A more continuous and robust W–Ni–Cu interface transports heat more effectively, including after irradiation.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have a lower void volume fraction than otherwise identically processed composites without Ni.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than otherwise identically processed composites without Ni.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites will retain greater mechanical durability after irradiation than otherwise identically processed composites without Ni.

Induction casting, arc-plasma casting, spark-plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, and vapor-deposition baselines generally exhibit interfacial defects and suboptimal thermal or mechanical performance.
Ni–Cu interdiffusion or reaction at elevated temperature may affect long-term performance.
